newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Japanese premier Hashimoto arrives in Singapore.
newsitem.headline: Japanese premier Hashimoto arrives in Singapore.

text.p: Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto arrived in Singapore on Sunday on the last stage of a five-nation tour of Southeast Asia that will culminate in a major policy speech on his country's ties with the region.
Hashimoto was greeted at Changi airport by Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong and then went on to a reception attended by several senior cabinet members, including Foreign Minister Shanmugam Jayakumar.
Eyewitnesses said Hashimoto, who flew in from the Vietnamese capital Hanoi, appeared to be wearing a bullet-proof vest.
Billed by Tokyo as a landmark push to take its relations with the region beyond the economic sphere, Hashimoto's tour has been overshadowed by the 26-day-old hostage crisis in Lima.

The crisis entered a more hopeful phase on Sunday as Peruvian authorities were prepared to send their chief negotiator to meet the leader of Marxist rebels holding 74 hostages inside the Japanese ambassador's residence.
Hashimoto was due to hold formal talks with Goh on Monday and then give a key policy speech before leaving on Tuesday.

The Japanese leader is expected to lay out his policy on the Asia-Pacific region and explain what aides call "the Hashimoto principle". Analysts expect the speech to signal a commitment to take on a greater leadership role in the region.
They say economically booming Asia is now entering a tricky phase with Chinese influence growing at a time of doubts about the long-term U.S. commitment to the region's stability.
"Japan is the most potent player in the region and therefore any enhancement of its involvement would be welcome," said one regional analyst, who declined to be identified.

In a full-page statement in Singapore's Sunday Times newspaper, Hashimoto hailed the success of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) in promoting stability and economic prosperity and predicted closer cooperation in future.
ASEAN groups Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam.

A Japanese Foreign Ministry spokesman on Saturday shrugged off suggestions by reporters in Vietnam that Japan's drive for security cooperation with ASEAN was aimed at building a strategic alliance as a balance against China.
"This visit was about enhancing Japan's ties with ASEAN," he said. "We believe that this will be conducive to creating peace and stability in the entire Asia-Pacific region."

During his tour, Hashimoto has met some of the most influential figures in the region. He held talks with Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad in Kuala Lumpur on Wednesday and then flew on to meet Indonesian President Suharto on Friday.
On Saturday, he touched down in Hanoi where he was received by Prime Minister Vo Van Kiet.
Hashimoto's talks with Goh are expected to concentrate on strategic Asian issues with the focus on economic development as the prime source of regional stability.
Goh was likely to urge Hashimoto to encourage continued growth of Japanese investment in the ASEAN region, which accounts for 16 percent of Japan's trade, one analyst said.
"Southeast Asia has great potential for further development and is in desperate need of more foreign investment," he said.
